source.title: Asymptotics of Random Feature Regression Beyond the Linear Scaling Regime
source.authors: Hong Hu; Yue M. Lu; Theodor Misiakiewicz

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own random-feature regression results on double descent and refines the account: peaks can arise from feature-matrix conditioning even without label noise, additional peaks can occur, and tuned regularization can eliminate the double descent.
record.gate_note: The paper also describes earlier results from cited work; those are not recorded as rows. Rows below cover the paper's own RFRR results, including explicit qualitative findings and plotted results. The numerical curves in Figures 2–4 are not tabulated.
record.test_reason: The paper derives sharp asymptotics for random feature ridge regression (RFRR, not a deep network) in the polynomial scaling regime and checks them numerically. Test error peaks at n = p when sweeping either p or n (Figs. 2 and 4), which bears on V3 and V4. The paper also analyses peak sources, extra peaks and optimal regularization (V6), and plots test error against the coefficient norm (V7). Double descent in RFRR was already known in the linear scaling (MM22). The main novelty is a new scaling setting, so T3 fits better than T5, although the V6 analysis adds T5-type qualifications.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors show RFRR follows R(n, p) ≈ max{R(n,∞), R(∞,p)}, a trade-off between approximation and statistical error, with a double descent at n = p in the critical regime κ1 = κ2, extending MM22 beyond linear scaling. They add four points. Coefficient norm gives a U-shaped curve. p/n → ∞ suffices to match KRR error. Overparametrization can hurt when under-regularized. Optimal regularization removes the peak. The claim that parameter count is a poor proxy is framed through prior double-descent work.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses asymptotic analysis and finite-dimensional numerical experiments for random feature ridge regression with fixed random features and ridge-fitted coefficients. It does not reproduce deep-network training or measure error over epochs.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior varies with regularization, noise and signal levels, the ratio of feature count to sample size, polynomial scaling regime, and whether regularization is optimized.
record.problems: The evidence concerns random feature ridge regression rather than deep networks. The formal results rely on high-dimensional polynomial-scaling assumptions and random high-frequency target coefficients. Several numerical outcomes are shown only in figures; the stated experiments average over 100 trials, but the error-bar definition is not given.
record.rows_left_out: No additional own results directly bearing on the listed versions were omitted. Results in cited prior work were excluded.

untested.parts: Deep-network model-size double descent; only RFRR is analysed.
Epoch-wise behaviour; no training dynamics are studied.
Deep networks and other model classes; only RFRR in the critical regime κ1 = κ2.
Model classes other than RFRR (and KRR as its p = ∞ limit).
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epochs and samples. Only the size axis is touched (Fig. 2: ∥âλ∥²/n is maximised at p = n where test error peaks).
Complexity measures other than the ℓ2 coefficient norm; model classes beyond RFRR.

missing.what: The statement that in under-regularized cases overparametrization can hurt and optimal test error is reached at p ≪ n.

missing.what: ∥âλ∥²/n peaks at p = n exactly where test error peaks: a complexity measure locating the peak on the size axis.
Figure 3 curves of test error versus p, n and SNR for several λ, showing peaks at small λ and monotone curves at optimal λ.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The setting is RFRR, a stylized lazy-regime two-layer model, under high-dimensional asymptotics with randomized high-degree target coefficients. Numerical checks use d = 50 or 100 and 100 trials, and curves are given only in figures. I changed the r8 verdict from limits_scope to supports, because V6 explicitly includes multiple peaks. I softened the r7 verdict from challenges to limits_scope, because the noise-free peak still comes from feature randomness (conditioning) and V6's 'variance' may cover that. Tranche changed from T5 to T3.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size double descent; the study analyzes random feature ridge regression, not deep networks.
Test error over training epochs or training time.
The result is for random feature ridge regression, not deep networks, and does not establish that more data hurts in other model classes.
Only random feature ridge regression is analyzed; other model classes are not tested.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
The study gives results for its RFRR setting and regularization choices, not a general characterization across model classes.
The reported effective-complexity comparison uses the squared coefficient norm in RFRR; other parameter-count corrections are not tested.

rows.subject: random feature ridge regression (RFRR)
rows.operation_detail: Analyze the test-error peak at the interpolation threshold under small regularization.
rows.measure: test error at the interpolation threshold
rows.note: The study attributes this peak to divergence of the feature-matrix conditioning number as the matrix approaches square.
rows.check: Analytic statement that the peak diverges as λ → 0+, i.e. its height depends on regularization. It is not separate evidence for V4; the V4 label should not cite it.

rows.subject: random feature ridge regression (RFRR)
rows.operation_detail: Analyze whether the interpolation-threshold double descent requires lower-degree signal or label noise.
rows.measure: test-error behavior at the interpolation threshold
rows.value: RFRR can still display double descent.
rows.note: The paper explains this occurrence by the conditioning number of the feature matrix, so the peak is not necessarily driven by label noise or variance.
rows.check: The text writes 'F<ℓ = ρε = 0' for the bias-term peak. Given the bias-variance decomposition, F>ℓ (which acts as effective noise) is probably meant, so the condition may be a typo in the source. The finding is that the peak persists without label noise, driven by feature-matrix conditioning.

source_check.correct: The source explicitly states F<ℓ = ρε = 0 and attributes an interpolation-threshold bias peak to feature-matrix conditioning. Relative to V6's source attribution, this is partial evidence requiring qualification, rather than an observed noise-or-variance-driven peak.
source_check.problem: The reported peak qualifies V6's attribution; the source's lower-degree condition must not be silently replaced with a high-degree condition.

rows.subject: random feature ridge regression (RFRR)
rows.operation_detail: Analyze additional peaks in the test-error curve.
rows.measure: test-error peaks at polynomial sample-size scales
rows.value: Additional variance peaks can appear, in addition to the peak at n = p.
rows.note: The text attributes these additional peaks to degeneracy of singular values associated with degree-ℓ spherical harmonics.
rows.check: V6 explicitly allows several peaks, so extra variance peaks at n ≈ d^ℓ/ℓ! support V6 rather than limit it. These peaks appear only for κ1 ≥ κ2 with large λ̄ and 1/ζ, and need F>ℓ or ρε nonzero.

rows.note: The paper states that optimally tuned regularization eliminates the double descent.

relation.reason: Its asymptotic results and numerical experiments directly test sample-wise and feature-wise double descent and regularization dependence.

tranche.reason: The paper extends random-feature regression asymptotics from linear to polynomial scaling and reports its own double-descent results in that setting.

source_check.notes: The source explicitly writes F<ℓ = ρε = 0; a possible typo does not authorize substituting F>ℓ. The λ → 0+ statements take that limit after the high-dimensional limit; commutation of these limits is left open.

statements.correction: Section 2.4: bias is defined with respect to label noise; a conditioning-related bias peak can occur at n = p for small λ; the explicit condition is F<ℓ = ρε = 0; higher-degree target components act as effective additive noise. This qualifies the attribution component of V6.
statements.problem: The RFRR bias-peak description is supported, but the challenges label overstates what this establishes against the compound V6 claim; zero label noise does not by itself exclude effective noise from higher-degree target components.
